source: Kahneman and Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk
finding: Certainty effect (Allais-style). People prefer a sure 2,400 to a gamble with higher expected value, but prefer the 33% gamble for 2,500 to the 34% chance of 2,400. This violates expected utility.
numbers: Problem 1: 82% chose B (2,400 sure) over A (2,500 at .33; 2,400 at .66; 0 at .01), N=72. Problem 2: 83% chose C (2,500 at .33) over D (2,400 at .34), N=72.
quote: people underweight outcomes that are merely probable in comparison with outcomes that are obtained with certainty
limits: Hypothetical choices, small student samples, Israeli currency. Majority pattern, not every subject.
agent_relevance: Background: a scaffold should not assume human-like choices follow expected value when a sure option is present.

source: Kahneman and Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk
finding: Common-ratio version of the certainty effect. Cutting both probabilities by a factor of four reverses the majority preference.
limits: Hypothetical money. Small N.
agent_relevance: Same ratio, opposite answer depending on scale: a consistency check for any agent.

source: Kahneman and Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk
finding: Non-monetary prizes show the same certainty effect, so it is not only about money.
numbers: Problem 5 (50% chance of a three-week tour vs a one-week tour for sure): 78% chose the sure tour, N=72. Problem 6 (5% vs 10% chance, same prizes): 67% chose the larger prize with lower odds.
limits: One prize type (travel), N=72.
agent_relevance: Effect is not about arithmetic alone; wording of outcomes matters.

source: Kahneman and Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk
finding: Reflection effect. Mirroring gains into losses flips risk attitude: risk averse for gains, risk seeking for losses.
numbers: Problem 3: 80% took the sure gain of 3,000. Problem 3' (-4,000,.80 vs -3,000 sure): 92% chose the gamble, N=95. Problem 13 (gains): 82% chose the split (4,000,.25; 2,000,.25) over (6,000,.25), N=68; Problem 13' (losses): 70% chose (-6,000,.25), N=64.
limits: Reflection holds for the problems listed; I read only the clearly aligned rows of the results table.
agent_relevance: Same problem with opposite sign gives opposite answer: a sign-consistency test for a scaffold.

source: Kahneman and Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk
finding: Isolation effect. People drop components shared by all options, so identical final prospects get different choices depending on how they are presented.
numbers: Problem 10 (two-stage game, .25 chance to reach stage two): 78% chose the sure (3,000) branch, N=141, although final outcomes equal Problem 4 where only 35% chose the 3,000-at-.25 option. Problems 11 and 12 (bonus of 1,000 vs 2,000 added first): 84% chose sure +500 (N=70) but 69% chose the gamble -1,000 (N=68), though final wealth is the same.
limits: Hypothetical. Presentation differences only.
agent_relevance: Supports normalising a problem to final outcomes before choosing.

source: Kahneman and Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk
finding: Overweighting of very small probabilities: both lottery tickets and insurance are attractive.
numbers: Problem 14: 72% chose a 1-in-1000 chance of 5,000 over a sure 5, N=72. Problem 14': 83% chose a sure loss of 5 over a 1-in-1000 chance of -5,000, N=72. Problem 9 (probabilistic insurance): 80% said no, N=95.
limits: Small sample. Later work (description-experience gap) finds rare events underweighted when learned from experience.
agent_relevance: Rare-event probabilities stated in text are over-treated by humans; an agent could be tested for the same.

source: Kahneman and Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk
finding: Theory structure. Two phases, editing then evaluation. Value function on gains and losses from a reference point: concave for gains, convex for losses, steeper for losses. Probabilities become decision weights pi(p) with pi(p) above p for small p, subcertainty and subproportionality.
numbers: Editing operations: coding, combination, segregation, cancellation, simplification, dominance detection. V(x,p;y,q)=pi(p)v(x)+pi(q)v(y) for regular prospects. Loss aversion argued from the rejection of symmetric (x,.50;-x,.50) bets, with v(x) < -v(-x).
limits: No numeric parameters in the paper. Editing phase is described, not formally tested; critics say the theory fits choices, not process. Weight function not well behaved near 0 and 1.
agent_relevance: The editing phase looks like a normalisation step in a scaffold: restate the problem, cancel shared parts, check dominance.

source: Tversky and Kahneman (1992) Advances in prospect theory: cumulative representation of uncertainty
finding: Cumulative prospect theory (CPT) uses rank-dependent cumulative weights, handles many outcomes and uncertainty, and gives a parametric form: value x^alpha for gains, -lambda(-x)^beta for losses, weight w(p)=p^g/(p^g+(1-p)^g)^(1/g). It predicts the fourfold pattern.
numbers: From memory, not verified this session: median alpha=beta=0.88, lambda=2.25, gamma (gains)=0.61, delta (losses)=0.69; 25 graduate students; certainty equivalents for about 28 gain and 28 loss prospects.
limits: Full text could not be opened (mirrors returned HTML or 404). Numbers are recalled, check before citing. Small N, median fits, hypothetical choices.
agent_relevance: This parametric form is what the LLM studies below fit.

source: Brown, Imai, Vieider and Camerer (2020) Meta-analysis of empirical estimates of loss aversion
finding: Large cross-discipline meta-analysis. Mean loss aversion is near 2, a little below the 2.25 of the original CPT fit.
numbers: 607 estimates from 150 articles (1992-2017); mean lambda = 1.955, 95% interval [1.820, 2.105]. Few study features strongly predict differences.
limits: Abstract only, read through Europe PMC; full paper not opened. Estimates depend on elicitation method.
agent_relevance: Human benchmark (lambda about 2) for comparing LLM fits.

source: Ruggeri et al. (2020) Replicating patterns of prospect theory for decision under risk (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: Direct multinational replication of the 1979 items. Core effects replicate, with some attenuation.
numbers: n=4,098, 19 countries, 13 languages. 94% of items replicated; 12 of 13 theoretical contrasts replicated; 100% in some countries. Heterogeneity between countries and individuals.
quote: empirical foundations for prospect theory replicate beyond any reasonable thresholds
limits: Abstract only (full text behind a login redirect). The one contrast that failed is not named in the abstract. Hypothetical choices.
agent_relevance: Human benchmark is robust on average, but people differ a lot.

source: Hertwig, Barron, Weber and Erev (2004) Decisions from experience and the effect of rare events in risky choice
finding: Boundary condition. When outcomes are learned by sampling, people underweight rare events, the opposite of prospect theory. This is the description-experience gap.
numbers: Abstract: description choices overweight rare events; experience choices underweight them. Causes explored: small samples and recency.
limits: Abstract only. Exact choice percentages not read.
agent_relevance: An agent that estimates probabilities by sampling (simulation, tool calls) may underweight rare events.

source: Does holding decision-makers accountable make them less loss averse? A three-study replication attempt (2026)
finding: Failed replication of Vieider: accountability did not reduce loss aversion in two new experiments or in a close direct replication with almost double the sample.
numbers: Third experiment: Bayesian test gave substantial evidence for no difference between conditions.
limits: Abstract only. Authors say the loss aversion measure may be unsuitable.
agent_relevance: Instruction-level debiasing of loss aversion is not reliable; links to the debiasing subfields.

source: Horton, Filippas and Manning (2026 revision) Large language models as simulated economic agents: what can we learn from Homo silicus?
finding: Section 2.4 summarises Oprea (2024b): the fourfold pattern also appears with no risk (the mirror condition), suggesting prospect theory partly reflects complexity. The authors then simulate it with LLMs.
numbers: Oprea design: 100 boxes, gain or loss of $25, probabilities .1,.25,.75,.9. LLM replication: $50 endowment, 19 probabilities, 5 models (GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4o, Claude-Haiku-3, Claude-Sonnet-3.5, DeepSeek), 94 agents, 10 repetitions, 15,200 observations, temperature 1. Lottery and mirror conditions moved together; weaker models and 'very bad at math' personas showed the X-shaped pattern; stronger models mostly gave the expected value.
limits: Simulation by the authors. Critics (Banki et al. 2025) say human subjects misread the mirror task. Pattern in LLMs depends on model and persona.
agent_relevance: Prospect-like distortions in an LLM seem to track available reasoning effort, so explicit computation should shrink them.

source: Oprea (2024) Decisions under risk are decisions under complexity, as summarised in Horton et al.
finding: Competing explanation: the fourfold pattern persists in a no-risk mirror condition, so it may come from heuristic responses under cognitive limits, not probability weighting.
numbers: Mirror condition: all boxes opened, payoff equals expected value; pattern still appeared in aggregate. Banki et al. (2025) reply that subjects were confused.
limits: Second-hand through Horton et al.; the original paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: If distortions come from complexity, decomposition and explicit arithmetic in the scaffold should reduce them.

source: Ross, Kim and Lo (2024) LLM economicus? Mapping the behavioral biases of LLMs via utility theory
finding: Fits Tversky-Kahneman value and weighting functions to LLM certainty equivalents. GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo show no probability distortion for gains; GPT-4 Turbo distorts losses more than humans.
numbers: 56 game settings, 100 samples per setting, temperature 1. Only GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo passed a monotone switching-point competence test. Across tasks LLMs had weaker loss aversion than humans and similar risk aversion. GPT-4 Turbo risk seeking for losses like humans; GPT-4 risk averse for losses.
quote: neither entirely human-like nor entirely economicus-like
limits: Only two models passed the competence test; behaviour inconsistent across settings. Numeric parameters are in figures, not text.
agent_relevance: LLM prospect parameters differ from human ones and are unstable.

source: Ross, Kim and Lo (2024) LLM economicus? (prompting interventions)
finding: Telling GPT-4 to be risk or loss averse barely moves behaviour; on losses the value function became more concave, the opposite of intended. Examples work better than labels.
numbers: Direct prompting, chain-of-thought, one-shot and two-shot on GPT-4. One-shot examples altered behaviour for risk; two-shot gave mixed results; role-playing a teenager lowered loss aversion with no change in risk aversion.
limits: One model (GPT-4).
agent_relevance: A stated instruction such as be cautious will not reliably set risk behaviour; show worked examples instead.

source: Jia et al. (2024) Decision-making behavior evaluation framework for LLMs
finding: Estimates risk preference, probability weighting and loss aversion for ChatGPT-4-Turbo, Claude-3-Opus and Gemini-1.0-pro using multiple choice lists, and compares them with a human sample.
numbers: Three series of choice lists; 300 repetitions per model, context free. All three LLMs risk averse (mean risk parameter above 0). ChatGPT had the lowest loss aversion and a weighting parameter above 1 (underweights unlikely events, unlike humans). Claude: lower risk aversion, higher loss aversion, overweights small probabilities. Table 5 loss aversion for LLMs is roughly 1.3 to 1.5 for one model versus a human sample of about 2.2 to 6.3 (table text garbled, treat as approximate).
limits: Their utility form differs from CPT (exponential weighting). Older model versions. Parameter table hard to parse.
agent_relevance: LLMs are generally less loss averse than people; adding demographics to the prompt shifts the parameters (a fairness risk).

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: GPT-3 on decisions from description. It showed 3 of the 6 biases identified by Kahneman and Tversky: framing, certainty effect, and overweighting of small probability differences (1% vs 2% counts more than 41% vs 42%). Not human level.
numbers: Over 13,000 problems from a choice benchmark. Only the largest model (Davinci) beat chance: t(29134) = -16.85, p<.001, but below humans: t(29134) = -11.50, p<.001. Three smaller models were at chance.
limits: GPT-3 era model only; three of six biases absent.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that prospect-like biases appear in LLMs through language alone.

source: Suri et al. (2023) Do large language models show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5
finding: GPT-3.5 shows a framing effect and an endowment effect on the same prompts given to people.
numbers: Framing: ChatGPT rated drug efficacy 5 in all 11 positive-frame trials and 4 in all 11 negative-frame trials (1-7 scale); humans 5.2 (CI 5.03-5.37) vs 4.6 (CI 4.35-4.85), t(80)=3.86, p<.001. Anchoring: low vs high anchor, ChatGPT t(58)=8.78, humans t(58)=5.55.
limits: ChatGPT outputs nearly identical across trials (no variance); small human sample. Loss aversion as the cause is untested in the LLM.
agent_relevance: Loss-framed wording in a prompt will move an agent, so wording should be neutralised.

source: Chen, Liu, Shan and Zhong (2023) The emergence of economic rationality of GPT (PNAS)
finding: GPT makes largely rational budget decisions in risk, time, social and food tasks, with a higher revealed-preference rationality score than humans.
numbers: 95, 89, 81 and 92 of 100 GPT observations had no GARP violations (CCEI=1) for risk, time, social and food. 347 US human subjects in a parallel experiment; GPT CCEI higher in all four domains (p<.01). GPT risk parameter closer to expected-utility maximiser; preferences more homogeneous than humans.
limits: Budget-allocation tasks, not prospect-theory gambles. Tests consistency, not loss aversion.
agent_relevance: LLM choices can be more consistent than humans even when they do not match human risk attitudes.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Builds 13,465 prompts to test framing, status quo and other biases in admissions-style LLM decisions and tests mitigation prompts.
numbers: 13,465 prompts; framing tested with admit, reject and neutral frames. Awareness prompting reduces biased prompts in framing and status quo to 17.2% and 8.5% (as I read the two-column text).
limits: Partly read; not a direct prospect-theory test; text layout made some figures unclear.
agent_relevance: Self-debiasing prompts give some gain; links to the debiasing subfields.

source: Adam-Troian, Bonetto and Arciszewski (2025) Replicating patterns of prospect theory for territorial decision under risk
finding: Preprint extending the multinational replication to territorial decisions.
numbers: Only the title and year seen in a literature index; no numbers read.
limits: Not opened; included as a pointer.
agent_relevance: None until read.
